speechtext:
That Bill Q2 of the Senate for the relief of Hyman Stotland, the preamble of which has been reported not proven by the select standing committee on miscellaneous private bills, be placed on the order paper, under standing order No. Ill for consideration in committee of the whole of this house at eight o'clock p.m. this day.

Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) moved the third reading of Bill No. 110, to amend the Dominion Notes Act.
Motion agreed to and bill read the third time and passed.

Hon. H. A. STEWART (Minister of Public Works) moved the second reading of Bill No. 113, to provide for the construction and improvement of certain public works and undertakings throughout Canada.

Public Works Construction-Mr. Elliott
He said: Mr. Speaker, the general principle of this bill will, I think, prove acceptable to the house. It is introduced in answer to a general demand from various sources for the inauguration of a program of public works throughout the Dominion of Canada. The bill has the threefold purpose of providing employment over a considerable period of time for those engaged in all lines of trade and activity connected with the construction business; of providing useful public services in the way of buildings and other structures, and of stimulating others to go and do likewise in connection with the building trades.
There is attached to the bill a schedule which sets out in detail the works that are proposed, with a general item which is calculated to enable the departments to put every public building in the Dominion of Canada in first class repair, including painting, plumbing, heating, wiring and so on. Then there is a similar vote for improvements to wharves and other structures in the harbours. It has been found that some of these wharves are not adequate for present needs. Some of them require strengthening, owing to the increasing use of trucks which has resulted in heavier loads passing over the wharves, and a survey is being made with a view to bringing them up to present requirements. In addition recent storms on the Atlantic have made repairs necessary in many instances, and this vote will provide funds for these purposes.
I hope the general principle of the bill will meet with the approval of the house. I can understand that there may be some discussion as to the details and as to some of the items in the schedule, but I submit the bill for the approval of the house with the hope that we may get into the schedule as soon as possible.

Mr. Speaker, I have looked over the various sections and the schedule of this bill with some care, and I think there is a great deal to be said in favour of the principle of getting away from the policy of unemployment relief which the government has been following, against the wishes of hon. members on this side of the house, for practically the last four years, and adopting a principle which at any rate is an improvement on what they have been doing.
First of all may I point out to you, Mr. Speaker, and to the house that at the special session of 1930 the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) proposed two methods for relieving unemployment. One was to raise the tariffs and the other was to vote $20,000,000 to assist in unemployment relief. The right
hon. gentleman will bear in mind, as I am sure other hon. members of the house will, that at that time it was urged by my right hon. leader and by many other members from this side of the house that so far as the expenditure of public money on public works was concerned, it was not proper to do that without submitting estimates to the house by way of a supply bill. That was the argument advanced at the special session of 1930, and while I am on that point I might read what was said by the Prime Minister at that time. When reference was made to the fact that we were getting away from the usual practice of calling for tenders and having the minister explain the different items in the house, the Prime Minister said:
I think the safeguards of the Public Service Act with regard to tenders are sufficient guarantee as to the money being expended.
I regret to find that these safeguards are being taken away to a large extent under the present bill.
No.

My hon. friend says not, but I think I can convince him in this regard as I was able to convince him once before, I think, when he contradicted me as to the relative proportion of the amounts going to the different ridings. I think I can show him once more that he is mistaken and that I am correct.
That was what the Prime Minister said at that time. Now I am going to endeavour to show that in this bill we are getting away from one of the greatest safeguards that the taxpayers of this country have had in regard to public expenditures. Ever since confederation there has been a provision that it shall be the duty of the minister to invite tenders by public advertisement. I regret to see that in this bill the words "by public advertisement" have been omitted. The minister says we are not getting away from the old principle. I should be very glad if he would assure me now that we will get back to that principle and that he will have inserted in this bill the words " by public advertisement," because after all, that is the first objection to the bill as presented to the house.
What does that mean? The wording of the bill is very neat; it says:
-the minister or department of the government entrusted with the administration, management and execution of any of the works set forth in schedule A to this act shall invite tenders for the construction and execution of such works, and contracts for all such works and undertakings shall be awarded under the direction of the governor in council.
4300	COMMONS
Public Works Construction-Mr. Elliott
I ask the minister the reason for including the words "shall invite tenders" instead of using the clause that has been in the Public Works Act, the Public Service Act and the marine act ever since confederation, that it shall be the duty of the minister to invite tenders by public advertisement. That is the first objection to this bill, and I think it is a very serious objection. What is the advantage of doing it by public advertisement? I remember that a year or so ago the minister gave the house a long list of the newspapers in which these contracts were advertised. Everyone from one end of the country to the other who desired to tender on any of these works had an opportunity to do so when public advertisements of that kind were circulated. The result is different when private tenders are called for. I believe the minister will agree with me, and I believe that when I refer the Prime Minister to his words uttered in 1930 he will agree with me, when I state that public advertisement is the proper way in which to govern expenditures of this kind.
I submit there are sufficient safeguards in the act to enable certain work of a pressing nature to be carried on. Under the Public Works Act, as it now stands, public tenders shall be invited by public advertisement, except in certain specified cases. The first exception is that of a pressing emergency, where any delay would be injurious to the public interest. Under this heading would come any damage occasioned by a severe storm. We will suppose that part of a wharf had been washed away. Perhaps it would not be in the public interest to wait until the department could advertise for tenders. Steps would have to be taken immediately to protect the part remaining, and to repair the parts injured) Then, in the second place are those works which, from their very nature, may be more expeditiously and more economically executed by the officers and servants of the department. There are certain types of work which may always be done to greater advantage and more cheaply by the officers and servants of the department. I refer particularly to the repairing of old structures. For instance, in the work of resurfacing or recovering a bridge one cannot tell, until the work is opened up, in just what condition the timbers may be. The probability is that sueh work could be done more expeditiously and more economically by day labour.
I object strenuously to the repeal of that clause of the present law which states that where the estimated cost of any work is less than $5,000, and in the opinion of the minister in view of the nature of the work it is

not advisable to invite tenders, he need not do so. That has been the practice for over fifty years in the Department of Public Works. The amendment to the effect I have indicated was made in 1903 as the result of a practice which had been in vogue for the previous twenty years. Under those circumstances, for a work the estimated cost of which would be $5,000, one had to call for tenders. That was the rule, except in the case of an emergency or in connection with a work which could be done more economically and expeditiously by day labour or in some other way.
But what is the change now proposed? My greatest objection to the bill is that it contains these words:
Provided that no one work or undertaking certified by the chief engineer of the Public Works department to involve an expenditure in excess of $25,000 shall be authorized by the governor in council except on contract based on tenders.
What -is the change? All the works ranging from $5,000 to $25,000 may now be let without tender. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, and through you this House of Commons if hon. members think such a change is in the best interests either of the government, the parliament or the people of this country who must pay the bills. What can happen under that change? May I call the attention of hon. members to the fact that while in the schedule appear large contracts for which tenders will have to be invited, over one-third of the items appearing therein range between $5,000 and $25,000. I repeat that over a third of the items come in that class, and it means that we are increasing five times over the value of the works which may be done without calling for tenders.
As I pointed out previously all the leeway the minister requires is that provided -in cases of emergency and in cases where in his opinion or in the opinion of the governor in council the work could be done more expeditiously and economically by day labour. To make a change as sweeping as I have indicated at a time like this is, I submit, not in the interests of the people concerned. I say to the minister that the greatest protection he can have is the protection given him through being compelled to call for 'tenders between $5,000 and $25,000, as obtains at the present time. He kn-ows as well as anybody who has been associated with the Department of Public Works that where works are let without tenders and in cases where the minister in charge is not obliged to let contracts to the lowest tenderers, he is subjected to all the -influences of urgent friends, and some

Public Works Construction-Mr. Elliott
who are not such good friends, wiho aTe trying to obtain contracts by private tender instead of by public advertisement.
I urge upon the Prime Minister who introduced the bill and upon the minister now in charge of it the necessity of going back to the old rule which for over fifty years has been in force and has given satisfactory service. To make a change of this kind under present conditions is not advisable-and I make that statement altogether apart from certain clauses and general votes contained in the schedule. There are some large amounts mentioned in the schedule. For instance, there is the amount of $500,000 to supplement where necessary specific amounts hereinbefore provided, upon the authority of the governor in council. I say the item should not be put in that way. Then, there is another item of $2,000,000 for public buildings generally, improvements, additions, fittings and so on. Then, there is the vote for $2,000,000 coming under the Department of the Interior. These moneys are to provide for the construction and development of public buildings, camp sites, electric light and telephone systems, highways, trails, water and sewer systems, recreational areas, wharves, river protection works, and so on. The lump sum of $2,000,000 is indicated in the schedule, but there are no definite items stating where the moneys will be expended.
Another blank cheque.

Such an arrangement is
not, I submit, in the interests of the people, it is not in the interests of the department and will cause great inconvenience to the minister. Perhaps the minister will remember the objections made by hon. members on this side of the house who urged that the moneys being spent should be authorized by way of a supply hill. In 1932 we had the rather remarkable spectacle of having items tabled for harbours and rivers. While the expenditures there involved did not run into sums as large as the ones now under discussion, the fact remains that apparently no hon. member knew about those items until the session was over. Those schedules were preoared as part of the unemployment relief scheme. When you came to look over the bill, while in the recital it was mentioned that there was no political significance in it, yet when you examined the amounts you found that they were about six times as large in the ridings represented by government representatives as in the ridings not so represented. The same characteristic applies to this schedule.

You are
not complaining about that surely, after eight and a half years of the same treatment.

My hon. friend knows
perfectly well that there was not eight and a half years of the same treatment, and nobody knows it better than he does. He will not find the members who are sitting with him on that side of the house backing him up in that statement, because after all there are every year certain items of general public works that require to be done and that cannot be avoided no matter what the constituency may be. I do not think the hon. member for York-Sunbury is very serious when he makes that suggestion in the way he does, and I know perfectly well he will not get many to back him up in that statement.

My hon. friend the exminister was good enough to keep me on the waiting list for four years, and it was only three months before the election that he brought down $48 000 for a post office in my native town of New Glasgow.

But my hon. friend got
it, didn't he?

Yes, I got it-election
bait.
Yes, you did.

But only when you were
afraid to keep it back any longer.

And my hon. friend was
polite enough at the time to say that he had received very fair treatment. He will remember that, I think.
I did thank him, yes.

If my hon. friend from
Pictou means by his interjection to suggest that you should raise these amounts that can be let without tender from under $5,000 to over $25,000, I am surprised at him because I do not think that is his idea of good business.

I did not say anything
whatever in regard to that point. You are barking up the wrong tree.

Then that is perfectly all
right. I find in looking over this list of public works for Ontario, and I am referring particularly to Ontario because I think some of my colleagues will deal with some of the other provinces, there is about seven and a half million dollars to be spent in ridings represented by government candidates, and $2,747,000 to be spent in other ridings, of

Public Works Construction-Mr. Elliott
which amount about 12,250,000 is to be spent on a few items in the city of Ottawa which are necessary due to the fact that this is the seat of government.

Represented by
Liberals, though.
Oh, yes.

Why leave that
out?

I fancy that most of the ridings will be represented that way in a little while; it seems to be the trend of things. I do not want to labour the points that seem to me to be important in this bill, but a great mistake would be made in attempting to do these works without calling for tenders and without giving the contracts to the lowest tenderer. There has been no explanation given by the minister as to why that change has been made, not a word. Just as I warned the minister three years ago against the course that was being taken then of having public works done under unemployment relief without estimates being put through the house, I am just as much satisfied that he will find a year from now that my advice to-day is right as he is satisfied now that the advice I gave him three years ago was right.
The amount, Mr. Speaker, is a large amount, but I am not going to discuss that now. I quite agree with the opinion which I think is held on both sides of the house, that it is much better to be spending money for something that is needed in the country than giving it by way of dole to people, as has been done during the last three years. That is practically what we are on, the dole, and I want to congratulate the government on having experienced a change of heart in regard to their unemployment relief program. I understand that it has been decided that from now it is by a program of public works that they will afford unemployment relief.
There is another point about the bill that I do not like and that I should like to have cleared up, and that is as to the departments that will do the work. We have one department admirably equipped for constructing public works. I have the very greatest confidence in the efficiency of that department throughout, and I submit that works that are public works should be done under the supervision of the Minister of Public Works and by the officials of the Department of Public Works, instead of having them handed around from one department to another-works that are in reality public works.
Getting more patronage to certain ministers.

There is another objection that I make to the bill, and that is I do not think the practice should be followed of calling for tenders until the bill permitting the calling for tenders had passed the house. I understand that tenders are being called for, for some of these works before the bill has passed. I have no doubt that it will be passed, and that is a minor objection, but I do again protest just as strongly as I can against, first of all the abandonment of the public advertisements for tenders and secondly against the increase from less than $5,000 to over $25,000 in the amount that can be let without calling for tenders.

Mr. Speaker, I desire to add a brief word before the motion is put, and I rise now because I have to attend a committee meeting very shortly.
The first thing I should say is a word of congratulation to the government for having had the courage to embark on a very substantial program of public works in Canada for the relief of unemployment. I take it that the spirit behind this bill is the relief of unemployment in Canada, and to that extent I think we are all in agreement. I agree with what the ex-Minister of Public Works (Mr. Elliott) has said with respect to this system being an improvement over the dole system, and as far as I am concerned I hope the dole system is behind us forever, and that the people of this country will do something else than resort to the dole system.
With respect to what my hon. friend has said with regard to public tender, I do not understand that there is any departure being made from the principle that has been in existence for a good many years save and except with respect to those projects which may cost less than $25,000. I think ample justification can be found for the departure from the principle to which he has alluded.
I am not defending or criticizing that. What I desire to place upon the records of the house-I ask the minister in charge of the bill to give attention to this-is that consideration should be given to several factors. First of all, provision should be made in the contracts that wherever available and other things being equal, local labour should be employed. Second, wherever available and other things being equal, local materials should be employed. I have in mind the erection of public buildings in New Brunswick; our free stone should be used rather than materials imported from other com-

Public Works Construction-Mr. Rinjret
munities. Provision should be made to take care of these two matters. There is a third consideration which I desire to impress upon the government. One, two or three large contracting firms, such as I could name, should not be allowed to come in and get a monopoly of these contracts, even under the tender system. I think hon. members will agree that I am not approaching this matter in a narrow, parochial spirit; I do not want to be accused of that. I submit that the large contracting firms if given twelve or fifteen or more contracts under this program will be able to spread the overhead over all the projects and be in position to underbid the smaller contracting firms. I am anxious to see this work distributed, not only to local labour but to the local contracting firms. I believe such firms would give more sympathetic consideration to the local employment needs. I feel that they would give more consideration than the large, highly capitalized contracting firms, so many_ of which may turn out to be just subsidiary companies of American firms.

Mr. Speaker, I desire to say a few words on the second reading of this bill. I endorse what has been said by the former Minister of Public Works (Mr. Elliott) with regard to the tenders, publicity and the procedure of making contracts. My intention is to deal particularly with the city of Montreal. I may say that I am very grateful as a citizen of Montreal to the government for the public works which it intends to erect in our city, but I want to point out that even this amount of work will not wipe out the obligations towards the city. The unemployment situation in Montreal has been especially bad and it must be viewed from different angles. The government owes a large amount of money to Montreal for past accounts in connection with direct relief. On many occasions, both on the orders of the day and otherwise, I have attempted to have the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon) make a statement on this matter. Up-to-date the statements issued by this government or the Quebec government have not been very clear, It has simply been a game of throwing th,e onus from one government to the other or from both governments to the city of Montreal. Somewhat the same game has been played between the former and present administrations of the city and the unemployment commission. It would seem that it was nobody's and everybody's fault that these past due accounts have not been paid. Notwithstanding the vouchers which exist in connection with the contribution of 74726-272 J
the Ottawa and Quebec governments to the city of Montreal for direct relief, there is not the least doubt that a very large amount is due to the city. There is no excuse for not advancing immediately to the city at least a large proportion of the sums which are due. So far the reservations which have been made have made negotiation impossible. I know something of the difficulties in connection with the administration of the city and whether we or our friends or some other group are in power in Montreal, I take the stand, as a citizen, that both governments should come to the assistance of ithe city and pay at least a proportion of the arrears of direct relief. This matter is connected with this bill because the government takes the stand that the erection of these public works will bring the unemployment problem to a conclusion. These public works are all right but they will be insufficient to take care of our unemployment problem. The first thing which this government and the Quebec government should do is to pay a proportion of the arrears due to the city. The. city needs this money very badly and has had to make huge interest payments because it has not been available.
I have another submission to make in connection with this matter and I hope it meets with the approval of my confreres on this side of the house. The government is going to spend six or seven million in Montreal on public works but I know from personal experience that that will not solve the unemployment problem. It will alleviate it to a certain extent as a certain number of unemployed will be given work, but I do not agree with the government's intention to discontinue direct relief payments on July 15. The government is attempting to do away with its responsibilities in connection with the general problem of unemployment by bringing down this bill for the construction of public works. There are 35,000 heads of families now unemployed in Montreal and while I have not made a calculation I know that this program will not take care of all those unemployed. The stand which I have taken in this house and at public meetings when I was more closely connected with the municipal administration is that as long as there is one head of a family not provided with -work it is the duty of the governments to look after that family. Even though it is spending these millions of dollars, I do-not think the government should take the stand that it is through with contributing to unemployment relief. I agree with the principle that the erection of public works is better than direct relief, but if those works are not sufficient, the federal and provincial governments still have a responsibility. It is very
4304	COMMONS
Public Works Construction-Mr. Rinfret
unfair to consider that the problem is solved when only fifty or sixty per cent of the unemployed have been given employment. This is the stand I take in connection with this bill.
I am glad the Minister of Labour has extended the period of contribution by the federal government to July 15. I do not say that he has done this because of our demands, it is probably because of his own convictions. But I contend that there should be no limitation in these payments. The government is trying to reduce unemployment by the erection of public works but it is wrong to say that on a certain date it will not contribute otherwise. It should contribute otherwise if, notwithstanding this program of public works, there are still heads of families in need and out of work.
In connection with the public works designated for Montreal, I should like to make this statement. There is a considerable list, and I do not complain on that ground; but I see that provision is made for a public building, No. 101, which I understand is the customs build:ng. and No. 103, the postal terminal building, together with other works in the harbour of Montreal. If you look up the estimates of the last year that we were in power, 1930, you will find monej's voted for these or similar works.
And not spent.

Had we remained in power all these works which are now proposed, in a gesture of generosity towards the city of Montreal. would have been carried out four years ago: all these works would have been done if the estimates of the then government had been followed out.
This is an election spasm.

I do not desire to delay the second reading of the bill because I am not opposed to the principle of it, but I wish to repeat what has been said by the former Secretary of State and congratulate the Minister of Public Works and the administration upon h-aving, after four years of dilatory tactics, adopted the principle and policy which we on this side have been advocating for the last few years.
Say a kind word.

I think
my hon. friend from Parkdale had better go back to Toronto. The government is not only adopting the policy of public works, as we have advocated it, but is financing this policy exactly as we urged on this side through the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) and the hon. member for North Bruce (Mr. Malcolm) over a year ago. As I did the other day, when discussing the Dominion Notes Act, I wish to commend the Minister of Public Works and the Prime Minister for financing these works in the way they are doing. In the second place I wish to emphasize in the strongest possible terms the complete inadequacy of the amount provided to meet the situation. The present unemployment crisis in Canada cannot be met by the expenditure of 139,865,000 as under the terms of this bill.
Not a bad start.
But you should have started four years ago. You are starting something which those on this side will finish before another year is out.
Don't fool yourselves.

I wish
to warn the Minister of Public Works not to repeat in this legislation the catastrophic blunders of the 1930-31 legislation. He will recall that we asked from this side of the
house for certain precautions in connection with the estimates, certain precautions in connection with governmental control, certain precautions in regard to a national audit of every single cent spent; and we again warn the minister that we desire these precautions to be observed in regard to this legislation. I submit that under section 7 of the bill powers far too great are given to the minister himself.
I wish to identify myself with some of the remarks made by the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson). As a matter of fact I had already drawn up an amendment before the hon. member spoke, to provide that, should no additional cost be entailed in connection with such public works and undertakings as are authorized, they shall be financed and completed in local areas and that local labour shall be employed in so far as possible in the completion of such public works. So far as we in British Columbia are concerned, with the meagre allowance given us, we do not desire to have any of the moneys spent in the fabrication of material in the city of Montreal. I mention Montreal by way of illustration; it might be equally Toronto.
In this bill, out of a total of S39.865.000 that may possibly be spent, S32.224.200 is to be spent on large public buildings of steel, of brick, of stone construction, and on steel bridges, harbour works, piers, wharves and works of that kind whereas only $7,641,400 is to be spent on what you might call ordinary undertakings. Under this measure skilled artisans will certainly obtain employment, but I am afraid that the common day labourer will wait on the side lines watching these buildings go up. My criticism of this whole plan is that the ordinary day labourer is not going to find an opportunity for employment under it. I make these observations, I trust, in a constructive spirit. When the time comes to consider the items I shall make some suggestions to the minister in regard to certain projects in my own province of British Columbia. In the meantime I support the constructive suggestions of the former Minister of Public Works (Mr. Elliott) and the former Secretary of State (Mr. Rinfret) concerning this legislation. I have one further proposal to offer in regard to these public works; that the minister do what is done by the government of Great Britain in all such undertakings, that is in regard to the king's honour roll, that a certain proportion of ex-service men be employed on the contracts awarded. I think if the minister would include in his contracts these two provisos, the one I just
4306	COMMONS
Public Works Construction-Mr. Howard
mentioned and the other in regard to local labour and material as far as possible, then he will go a long way to meet the criticisms from different parts of the country.
I want to conclude as I commenced, by commending the administration for that in this eleventh hour of their political life they are embarking on this program, and by commending the Prime Minister for adopting at the same belated hour the suggestion for financing these works which we on this side of the house advanced years ago; and I trust that future administrations will enlarge it into a really comprehensive program of public works for the relief of unemployment throughout Canada.

I am not going to congratulate the government upon this program of public works that they have brought down to-day because I believe that if this government had done what they promised to do in 1930 this country would be in a different position from that in which it is to-day. I want to criticize two or three clauses of the bill, and then state the reasons why I do not think this distribution is equitable. It is admitted by everyone that during times of crisis like this people flock into the centres in order to be taken care of, even if they cannot get employment; therefore the unemployment situation is much more acute in the larger centres than elsewhere. In the province of Quebec we have four large centres. Montreal is our main centre, Quebec comes second in population, and Three Rivers and Sherbrooke vie with one another for third place, they are practically equal. We naturally think that Sherbrooke is third, and Three Rivers people think they are. Now if you examine the schedule here is the situation. In the city of Montreal it is proposed to expend $5,989,500, which is certainly not too much for the city of Montreal. In Quebec it is proposed to expend $1,722,500, that is in the districts immediately surrounding those centres. In Three Rivers the amount to be spent is $484,000 while in Sherbrooke, the third largest centre in the province of Quebec, they do not propose to spend one single nickel. I shall give some figures to show what the unemployment condition has been, and what conditions are in the city of Sherbrooke at the moment. But in the whole of those eastern townships of Quebec, consisting of eight counties federally and eleven provincially, only one work is proposed, that is in Farn-ham, in the constituency of the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Pickel), amounting

to $58,000. I think under those conditions I have a right to protest.
Population figures for the city of Sherbrooke as of last week show a total of 29,284. Taking into account the births during the year you find a net decrease in population during the past twelve months of 439 in spite of the unemployed coming into the city. In Sherbrooke we run a municipal kitchen to feed these people and keep them from starving. Our official figures of families on kitchen relief are as follows:

Yet in spite of these figures we find not a single nickel provided under this bill for the city of Sherbrooke, the hub of the eastern townships of Quebec, to aid in unemployment relief.
One further aspect of the matter to my mind is more impressive than all the others; and I say this directly to the Prime Minister. I want him to realize the situation. I am one who believes that in a city the proprietor is what the Prime Minister termed the sheet anchor of the Canadian municipality. In Sherbrooke according to the last census we had 29,284 people, and in 1930 there were 2,975 proprietors; in other words 10-3 per cent of the people owned their homes. In 1931 the number of proprietors had dropped to 2,876; in 1932 to 2,596 and in 1933 to 2,233. In other words in a two year period, due to foreclosures and people losing their homes, there was a reduction of 643 in the number of property owners. If you carry that percentage on for another few years you might as well consider Sherbrooke in the class with a Russian municipality. I draw this to

Public Works Construction-Miss Macphail
the attention, of the committee because I think the distribution is absolutely unfair and shows no consideration for the needs of these centres in the province of Quebec.
I also criticize this bill in respect of the methods adopted for carrying out its objects. The word " public" 'is left out before the word " tender." I do not believe that this government or any government has any right to go on with a construction program without calling for public tenders. As this stands at present the government can call for private tenders or any other kind and go ahead and let contracts-
In the Tory fashion.

The proper way to do this is by public tender. The old legislation provided that for works costing less than $5,000 the minister had the right to use his judgment and go ahead without public tender. The figure has not merely been raised from $5,000 to $25,000, but the bill says "in excess of $25,000." Then it goes on to qualify that, it provides that an expert in the department shall estimate the cost. If he estimates it as not in excess of $25,000, they can go ahead without calling for tenders. That simply means that if their estimate should over-run, we will say, an ordinary percentage up to $35,000, the government propose to carry on the work without calling for tenders.
Then I do not see any provision with regard to the fair wage clause. I am exceptionally interested in that; I believe we should mention it in this legislation without leaving it to the fair wage act. I believe it should be put in here, because I am one of those who believe that if the wages you pay a man give him only a bare existence it is not of much benefit to the community. If you want to help your communities pay your men fair wages so they will have money to spend in order to make their fellowmen more prosperous.
Then I should like to direct the attention of the minister to the fact that Canadian companies are not specified. I know what has happened in the past; I know how United States companies evaded the law by forming Canadian subsidiaries to handle these contracts, and perhaps in prosperous times that might be countenanced. But in times of extraordinary stress I do not believe any United States company or any other outside company should be allowed to tender on or accept these contracts. As one other hon. member said a moment ago, we want Canadian labour to be used, Canadian companies to get these contracts and, so far as possible, local contractors and local labour to get their share of the work.
In closing I want to say that I agree entirely with those who have already spoken from this side of the house. After waiting three and a half years; after it has been found that the marketing bill will not remedy (the situation; after the government have failed to raise the prices of agricultural products; after the Prime Minister has failed to implement the promise he made from the public platform in Sherbrooke in 1930, that if he were elected people would rush back to their jobs and the country would be prosperous, and that if this did not happen we could blame the government; after all that I want to say that I am glad the government have adopted the policy which we call inflation. If they had proceeded three and a half years ago to deal with our currency as they propose to deal with it in the legislation brought down last week; if inflation had been brought about three years ago the situation would have been quitte different, and possibly this legislation would not have been necessary. I want to ask the Minister of Public Works, when he considers these items, to give particular attention to the large centres of the province of Quebec, and to give Sherbrooke its fair share in relation to Montreal, Quebec and Three Rivers, since we do not wish to be discriminated against.
Miss AGNES C. MACPHAIL (Southeast Grey):	Mr. Speaker, I would not have had
anything to say had it not been that the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie) rose a short time ago and said that this program, or perhaps a more extensive program, had been proposed by the Liberal party. The number of things the Liberal party claim to have sponsored is to me amazing and amusing. They suddenly become the exponents of a publicly owned bank; they say they were the .people who advocated a central bank, though I always understood that we were the people who converted them. I think everyone who sits in the house or in the press gallery will remember that over and over again the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote) suggested a public works program on a large scale financed with new money, that is, money issued without interest against the general assets of the people. I do not think one needs to argue the point. I might say to His Majesty's loyal opposition that if they had really wanted to bring in a program of public works for the relief of unemployment they' had an opportunity to do so before the election of 1930. I really think the Liberals were defeated then because of the depression and their inadequate methods of dealing with it. If they knew then what should be done it
4308	COMMONS
Public Works Construction-Miss Macphail
is a wonder they did not do it. At any rate, while those who sit in the southeast corner are very modest when the government bring in their programs, and do not like to rise too often and say, " Thank you very much"- or, as someone suggests, "We told you so"

 still I think it is going too far when the hon. member for Vancouver Centre claims credit for the Liberal party for suggesting that such a program be inaugurated. The order paper to-day carries a resolution standing in the name of the hon. member for Macleod, as follows:
That, in the opinion of this house, in view of the large number of unemployed, and with the necessity of increasing the purchasing power of the people, it is expedient that the government give immediate consideration to the inauguration of a large scale program of public works to be financed by a direct issue of non-interest bearing dominion notes.
Actually, if we enforced the rules as severely as they are enforced at times, we could not discuss the bill now before us because the subject matter is already before the house in this resolution, which was put on the order paper by an hon. member sitting in this corner.
I do most heartily congratulate the government upon bringing in a program of .public works. It is four years late, but at any rate it is being brought in now and is being financed in what I believe to be the correct manner. The program should have been larger; I think this is only a beginning, and that still larger programs will be brought in to be financed in the same way. I am sure the government will not appreciate my prolonging my congratulations, so I will bring that part of my remarks to an end. I think at this time we could easily stand a program calling for the expenditure of $100,000,000 rather than $40,000,000, financed in just the same way, because we have been deflated much more than $100,000,000, and there is no reason why we should not reflate to that extent, if people like the word "reflation" better than another that might be used. However, undoubtedly even this small program, amounting to $40,000,000, will do a great deal to relieve unemployment. At least it will put $40,000,000 of purchasing power in the pockets of the people and to that degree at least will help business.
I am sorry this program is not larger; I think we could have stood a very much larger one. I could have said $200,000,000 instead of S100,000.000, but perhaps we had better put it at the latter figure. We are spending only a small amount now. I look for larger programs in the future; I think they are

inevitable, and I think they will be financed in the same way.
As a last word I want to say to the hon. member for Vancouver Centre that I think he has claimed for himself and his associates about all the credit he had better try to claim this session.

Mr. Speaker, I am moved by somewhat conflicting emotions as I survey this vain attempt on the part of the government to save themselves from political extinction. That is what it means. They have one foot in the grave, and this is a great lunge to try and keep the other foot out. Of course it is claimed that this program is meant to relieve unemployment, and no doubt there is something to be said in that regard, but just how much of it will go for that purpose is another matter. It is something like the money spent for grasshopper bait; how much went for Grithoppers and how much for grasshoppers? No doubt this also will do away with the dole, in some little measure at least. Are we contemplating the expenditure of a great deal of money, nearly $40,000,000, for the purpose of affecting the coming federal election? That is what it is for; there is no use getting away from it. And it does not say very much for our criticism if we let them get away with it without pointing out that fact. And then to think of the stupidity of the government who seem to have the idea that such action will save them. Why, the deeper they are in the mud the farther they will get into the mire via this route. Have we been living all our lives with our heads buried in the sandpile so that we do not recognize these things when governments attempt to do them? We do not need to go back to antiquity to find it out. On the Prescott highway, part of that system of the King's highways, we saw men lined up like bees around honey and pretending to be working the day before the election. And out in Saskatchewan there were white men, black men, Indian boy graduates-all kinds of men, old and young, working on the roads only the week before and during the week of the election. How did they vote? Most of them just voted to soak the government that much harder. They took and earned their money and then put the boots to them afterwards.
That kind of blind failure has been this government's record, from its inception. Every move has been more stupid than the one preceding; each move has been non-effective in whatever purpose it set out to accomplish -and this is the hugest one of the lot. There

Public Works Construction-Mr. Motherwell
was a time in my early political career when, from a political standpoint, I would have been very much alarmed at this procedure;
I would have been afraid that the government would scoop in everybody and get all the voters within their toils. But to-day, even if they doubled the expenditures outlined in this bill, I would be quite composed, so far as that angle of the matter is concerned, because I know that their action will only result in the greater downfall of the government, when it comes. So we do not need to be alarmed at that.
Another matter which gratifies me is that recent events have shown that the people of Canada are not on the bargain counter. They are going to vote as they wish. They are going to take advantage of the secrecy of the ballot if the returning officers do not open their ballots as some of them did in Ottawa at the last election. They will vote, they will take advantage of what is supposed to be the secrecy of the ballot and in other respects they will govern themselves accordingly. There is no use haranguing the government. It is said that all governments do a little bit of this kind of thing prior to the elections. I do not admit that. But, for the sake of argument, supposing I do admit it;
I suppose it is only natural that one should dress up and brush up before he presents himself to the people at an election. Put on your best clothes, have your front yard swept up, and your backyard ditto. Maybe a little of that is only natural. But the present wholesale attempt, with no pretence at saying that the purposes behind it are not as I have indicated-well, it is just too much for me to swallow at one gulp, and without protest. I am not making these statements because there are no appropriations for my constituency; as a matter of fact, I do not know whether there are or not.
Not a dollar.
Hear, hear.

It is unfortunate that the minister who prepared these appropriations did not first consult the hon. Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon) and refer to the dole lists, in order to distribute this money in localities where it is most needed. Such a method would have been fairer and at least it could have been said that the government's object was purely to relieve distress.
Since 1930, sir, I have earnestly requested the hon. Minister of Public Works to erect a post office at L'Assomption.
That is a fact.

I think it
is not a matter of luxury, sir. The building is supported on all sides by props which this government has had placed there instead of rebuilding it.

It will
crumble like the government.

The town of
L'Assomption had to resort to the dole. On many occasions I requested that the post office, which is in ruins, as you may judge by this photograph, be rebuilt.

Show it
to the government.

I forwarded
a copy to the hon. minister at the time-

He did
not bestir himself.

-and he replied as follows:
While I fully agree with you and appreciate the fact that the building in its present condition must present anything but a pleasing appearance, I regret we have no appropriation to which the reconstruction of this building could be charged. I have however, made a note of the matter and it will receive every consideration when the estimates are being prepared for the ensuing fiscal year.
This was on November 29, 1932.
Mr. CASGRAIN (Translation) [DOT] He forgot about it.
Public Works C o?istruction~
COMMONS -Mr. Seguin
Who signed that?

The hon.
Minister of Public Works (Mr. Stewart). He certainly lost his memorandum because in quoting this item to relieve the unemployed, he forgot to provide for the reconstruction of the post office at L'Assom.ption which is crumbling; the Liberals, therefore, will be obliged to rebuild it as soon as they assume power.
Hear, hear.

I regret also
that the hon. minister has also lost sight of many other requirements affecting rural constituencies and particularly the county which I have the honour of representing in the house. The tobacco industry in my county is of primary importance and our farmers who are in distress requested, at various times, warehouses, so as to preserve their tobacco in good condition and enable them to market it advantageously. I earnestly requested the erection of such warehouses and I again do so now, if it is not too late; it could be included in this last item of the amounts to be expended:
To supplement where necessary specific amounts hereinbefore provided upon the authority of the governor in council.
Perhaps this paragraph could be altered; this amount of $500,000 would be increased, a few million dollars could be added to provide for various other requirements that the hon. minister forgot in the schedule.
Hear, hear.

Thus the post office at St. Lin; tobacco warehouses at St. Jacques-I'Achigan, St. Esprit and even at Joliette could be erected. The minister did not do so, he did not inquire in what localities this money could be utilized.
He is not a connoisseur in tobacco!

Moreover, it is urgent that a bridge be constructed at one end (bout) of " File Jesus," on the Jesus river. This bridge would link Montreal to the eastern part of our province, at the village of Charlemagne.

Quite so, the Charlemagne bridge.
, SEGUIN (Translation): The construction of this bridge would give work to a great number of unemployed in the adjacent counties. It would have been timely to construct this bridge, but it slipped the hon. member's mind. I could point out numerous urgent

undertakings in my county. The hon. minister is aware that a dam was requested on the Assomption river, so as to raise the water to its regular level and thus draw to its shore much wealth. The government promised, at the time, to give it their serious consideration, however, this promise became a dead letter, and when work is being distributed, the government rather think of other counties to which large sums of money are granted. I do not envy my colleagues who reside in the neighbourhood. We obtained, at St. Jacques-I'Achigan, under the Liberal regime the construction of a very attractive post office which cost $28,000. I note that $48,000 is appropriated for such a building at Berthier. I wish to congratulate my hon colleague from Berthier-Maskinonge (Mr. Barrette): however, I think the government could have set aside, out of the large amounts which it expends in certain localities, some funds to provide for other localities which have been completely ignored.
No justice exists.

I do not
wish to further delay the house, although endorsing the principle of the bill, I wished to point out that a grave injustice is being perpetrated in the distribution of moneys and that this bill seems rather introduced, not to win counties-it is futile-but in an endeavour to hold on to those which are in danger. I do not think that such a policy will succeed, in spite of all, the counties which are Liberal will remain so while the others will return to the Liberal fold.

Mr. Speaker, at the outset of the remarks I have to make on this bill, I want to say that I approve of the spending of $40,000,000 for public works because it does away with the direct relief system which has done so much harm to the country since the present government adopted that means of relieving unemployment in Canada. On June 19 the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) introduced this bill in the place of the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Stewart) who, as he said, was engaged in a patriotic duty. I want to take this opportunity of congratulating my genial friend, the Minister of Public Works upon the success he attained in the patriotic duty he was engaged in at that time. That success was considerable and has been heartily approved by the people of Ontario and the people of Canada in general. On that occasion the Prime Minister, answering a

Public Works Construction-Mr. Mercier
question asked by my right hon. leader (Mr. Mackenzie King), stated:
I can assure my right hon. friend that when he looks at it he will regard it as being the acme of patriotism, inasmuch as communities which have little claim except their adherence to the time honoured tenets of the great party which he has the honour to lead, have not been forgotten.
I want to deal with those words of the Prime Minister and endeavour to find out if there has been an equal distribution of this work among the different constituencies and divisions of Canada regardless of the political adherence of the representatives of those communities. I intend to deal particularly wi h Quebec as I am more or less familiar with that province. The former Minister of Public Works (Mr. Elliott) has dealt with Ontario and I shall not attempt to touch upon that province or any other province. In looking over the schedule of the bill I find that the first place in Quebec which is to be benefited by the provisions of this bill is Beauport, to which $20 000 has been allotted. Beauport is in a Conservative constituency. The next place is Berthierville, to which $48,500 has been allotted. I do not know whether this amount would have been allotted last week had the government known that the hon. member for Berthier-Maskinonge (Mr. Barrette) was going to leave his party when an important vote was taken in this house on Friday evening.

Does the hon.
member know that in the estimates for 1930-31. prepared by his hon. friends, provision was made for a building in Beauport?
No, I did not know that.

Why did you not carry it
out?

It
should have been carried out before. As has been said before, it is coming four years too late.
Better late than never.
I think you forgot Chicoutimi.
I mentioned it, $88,500.
I have $88,000 and I stick to it.
What about Edmonton?

If you want to go to Alberta, more than half the amount in the province goes to Calgary, the constituency represented by the Prime Minister. But to come back to Montreal. What struck me most in examining this schedule was that most of the amounts were items that should have been in the main estimates rather than in this special measure for public works. We find that the sum of $200,000 is voted for an armoury for the 17th Duke of York's Royal Canadian Hussars, and that amount can be attributed almost to anyone. I have nothing to say in that regard. Then we find $2,000,000 for a public building addition. I suppose this is the new customs building on McGill street, Montreal. This site was acquired a great many years ago and a certain amount of work has been done on the lot. The pillars are there, the place has been fenced in, and it is only right that at this time something should be done to supplement the expenditure that has already been made there. The next amount, taking Montreal, is for the postal station at Notre Dame de Grace, $136,000, the site of which has already been acquired. In Notre Dame de Grace, in the coming elections, it is possible that there will have to be a new government candidate, be-
[Mr. J. A. Mercier.3
cause the member for the present constituency of Mount Royal does not reside in Notre Dame de Grace, nor does the member for St. Antoine reside there, so that there will be a new government candidate in this division when the next election, so ardently hoped for, comes along. There will be a new Conservative candidate, I say, and something must be done to ensure in the minds of the government the election of that candidate. Therefore we find the sum of $136,000 voted, to be spent on a postal station in this part of the city.
I represent one of the most flourishing cities in the province of Quebec, not quite as large perhaps as Notre Dame de Grace, but under the administration of my good friend the former Postmaster General we were lucky enough to have a post office built in the city of Outremont. But the amount was not anything like $136,000. I think it only amounted to some $40,000. I am sure that when consideration of this item comes up the minister will explain why so expensive a building is to be put up in this suburb of Montreal.
As to the postal terminal building, everyone who knows anything about Montreal is aware of what has taken place. We know that the site was acquired-that is mentioned here-but it was acquired by the former government. The sum of $1,800,000 is to be spent in putting up this building. We have nothing to say against that, we are rather commending the government for carrying out the program of the former administration. I am advised by the former Postmaster General (Mr. Veniot) that there was an item of $600,000 appropriated in 1930 to carry out this project but it was cancelled by the government.
The next item goes to prove what I said a moment ago, that many if not the larger number of items in this schedule should have been included in the main estimates, but this futile gesture is made by the government pretending to come to the relief of unemployment. This $534,000 for repaving of certain surfaces should have been in the main estimates. And further to show that the nature of this work makes it clear that it should have been placed in the estimates, we find that the last amount for the city of Montreal is for the application of two protective coats of paint on the steel structure of the harbour bridge. A bridge of the importance and value of the Montreal harbour bridge has to be painted every now and then. That is not a matter of special relief but an ordinary expenditure that should have gone into the estimates.

Public Works Construction-Mr. Mitchell
The next item is for the reconstruction of eleven raceways at the Windmill point pier, $339,000. Under the former administration a sum of $1,500,000 was voted to carry out this work, but that was cancelled and now this government comes along with its belated generosity and votes the meagre sum of $339,000. Then we have another amount of the same nature, certain protection works against sifting of filling material supporting grain elevator No. 3. This is a work that had to be done of necessity and there is no special commendation to be given to the government for putting it in this measure. The next amount for Montreal is a sum of $242,000 for raising of a fronting wharf, sections 38, 39 and 40. That is work that should come under the ordinary expenditures of the government and should have been in the estimates, it should not be placed here.
I want to add my word of blame, Mr. Speaker, of the government for the clause in this bill which allows the granting of contracts for sums not in excess of $25,000 without calling for tenders. With great surprise also we find nothing in this bill calling for the fair wage clause. We know what has been going on throughout Canada as regards wages paid-[DOT]
That is provided in our specifications for all works that we undertake and in all works that we do by day work we conform to the act.

Why do you not put
it in the bill? It is not stated in the bill.
It does not need to be in the bill because it applies to everything.

I just wish to make a few general observations on this bill. First I want to congratulate the government on launching this public works policy. I think it is sound in principle, and that in adopting it they have followed the lead given by other countries of the world in an endeavour to break the spell of this depression. I have no criticism whatever to offer in that regard.
Further, I think that the government should be congratulated particularly on the financial policy of using the nation's credit rather than borrowing money for this undertaking. I believe it is an experiment, and I have no criticism to offer as to their being cautious in launching such a policy. If it is successful and proves sound it can be extended to much of the work set in motion by the government in the future.
The work to be done in my own city, where rentals at the present time for offices used by the government amount to $52,000 a year, is a productive enterprise that will result in a large saving. With the self-liquidating provisions of the bill it will return to the people of this country the capital expenditure involved.
What I wish to bring to the attention of the government is the question of the fair wages policy. I am not unmindful of the fact that the fair wages act provides that:
Every contract made hereafter with the government of Canada for construction, remodelling, repair or demolition of any work shall be subject to the following conditions respecting wages and hours:
But in subsection 2 the act says that:
The provisions of this section shall not apply to persons employed in fabrication or manufacture of materials, supplies or equipment for use in the work contemplated where such fabrication or manufacture is carried on in any established plant or factory other than a plant or factory established for the purposes of the work contemplated.
Especially in view of the disclosures in the price spreads committee, I think the fair wages policy in connection with this work should be all-embracing. I believe the government should give leadership in this connection, should insist that every nut, bolt, screw and piece of wood or equipment that goes into this program should be fabricated or produced under fair wage conditions. Might I give as an example the furniture industry in this country, on which much light has been thrown during the past year. I think the government should insist that any furniture that goes into these buildings should be produced and manufactured under fair wage conditions, with -wages that provide for a standard of living at least equal to what we consider a fair Canadian standard. I leave that suggestion with the government, notwithstanding that the act eliminates these establishments where the fabrication takes place from the fair wages requirements. I believe it would be wise on the part of the government to extend the provisions of that act to bring these establishments within the compass of that policy in connection with this undertaking.
Then I believe that every job should be awarded by contract. I would not accuse the government of endeavouring to use any of this work for political purposes in the broadest sense-
No doubt they will do so.

-but I believe the safest way to overcome that evil is to insist that
4316	COMMONS
Public Works Construction-Mr. Mitchell
every undertaking set in motion shall be let by contract. Then in the big undertakings I believe that every subcontract should be registered with the government. I do not think that what are known as broker contracts should be permitted, where the main contractor gets the contract and then chisels the other contractors down to provide a profit for himself. I believe every contract of any kind or character that is awarded should be registered with the government in order to prevent, the intrusion of the broker contractor.
I believe also, Mr. Speaker, that the government should give a lead in regard to the establishment of the six hour day. I believe the main purpose of this legislation is to distribute purchasing power among the building tradesmen of this country, and in passing I may say that it is a fact that the building and construction industry is the real cesspool of unemployment. I think it is a fact that eighty per cent of the money expended in construction goes in wages, and in view of the fact that the policy of the government is to take people off relief I think it might be well to experiment with the six hour day. I believe we are going to get the six hour day whether we like it or not; it is just a question of time. I believe it is a sound principle, and it might be well for the government to give leadership in that direction. It might be argued that it is not practicable, but I would point out that it would not be necessary to have a break in the midst of the six hours for meals or anything else; if necessary you could run two shifts, and in that way you would spread out the work so that as much as possible might be given those who want to put their hands to some productive enterprise.
I hope this government will not make the mistake that has been made by the government of Ontario in connection with some of their construction work. They insisted that a man must be on relief before he could take advantage of the work. I believe there are hundreds and thousands of people who have made every effort, who have used up the savings of a lifetime, in order to stay out of the relief offices. I believe those people should be given some measure of recognition. It should not be necessary for a man to be on relief before he can get work under this program. My main interest is that as many men as possible should be given work under this policy. In connection with the subcontracts I should like to point out that through the letting of these contracts by broker contractors the employees themselves may be placed outside the provisions of the workmen's compensation laws, and even the TMr. Mitchell.]
fair wage policy of the government. That is why I believe the government should insist that all these contracts must be registered, so that every bit of work done should be carried on under the legislation that has been enacted for the protection of men and women engaged in the industrial life of this country.
In conclusion I want to congratulate the government on launching this policy. I be-lipve that in the next five years the respective governments will have to take an active part in launching building programs for the purpose of eliminating the slums of this country. I believe we might take a leaf out of the book of the British government, who launched an enormnu5 home building program partly financed by the government. I believe that if the interest rates do not come down policies will have 'to be formulated and set in motion by the respective governments of this country looking to the abolition of the slums and the provision of housing accommodation of the kind we think is necessary in the life of this country.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
With the alleged purposes of the measure as set forth by the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Stewart) I think all parties in the house will be in agreement. The threefold purpose, as the minister described it, was that of providing employment, providing useful public services in the form of buildings and other construction work, and stimulating activity on the part of others to do likewise. I call these the alleged purposes, because it seems to me that if they were the real purposes this measure would have been brought down many months ago instead of in the concluding hours of the session. The circumstance that the bill is brought down at this time within a few days of the prorogation of parliament. together with the sections of the bill itself, give one good reason to believe that the emergency referred to in its provisions is not so much one with respect to unemployment as it is an emergency with respect to the government's own position in appealing to the people, as they no doubt will, in the very near future. The bill has all the earmarks of a measure introduced for the purpose of assisting the administration in a general election. Parliament is asked to vote a public works program amounting to S40.000.000 on. the eve of a general election; that in a nutshell is what the measure is.
May I point out to the minister wherein I think an examination of the measure will reveal its political intent. In the first place, were this an unemployment measure introduced for

Public Works Construction-Mr. Mackenzie King
the purpose of setting an example to others and of stimulating employment, it would have been brought down long ago. I would remind the house that it was November 20 last when the Prime Minister publicly announced that during the course of the forthcoming session a program of construction of public works would be introduced. When I read the announcement, I thought, judging from what little knowledge I have of political affairs, and of -hon. gentlemen opposite, that it meant a general election at the end of the session, that the government was preparing the way for a program of public works to be put forward, not in the regular way in the form of a supply bill, to be voted as estimates for public works, but as a measure supposedly in aid of the unemployed. During this session I have watched pretty carefully to see just when this program would be brought down, and the longer it was postponed the more certain I became that it indicated the near approach of a general election. Several times during this session I asked the Prime Minister when we might expect this public works program. He gave one reason after another, or I should not call them reasons; I should say he gave one excuse or apology after another for the delay. Once he said the program was like Jonah's gourd, that it was getting larger and larger, and numerous demands were being made which he had to consider. Later on we were told that it would not do to have it suggested that he was seeking to bribe the people with their own money by bringing down the program while the elections in Saskatchewan and Ontario were under way. But I would point out, Mr. Speaker, that long before there was any announcement of an election in Ontario or Saskatchewan, long before those dates were fixed, there was ample opportunity for the government to have introduced this program.
As a matter of fact, if this program really was intended to assist the unemployed and stimulate industry, it Would have been brought down early in the session in the regular way, in the public works estimates, which would have insured proper control of the expenditure by this House of Commons. It is now almost July 1. As the minister knows better than anyone else, it takes a certain time to prepare plans for public works. Tenders have to be called for, or ought to be called for, and that takes more time. As a result we will be fairly well along in the year before this particular program, which is intended to take the place of the dole, will be in operation. What has -been happening in the meantime according to the government? The government has 74726-273
been telling us that in the meantime conditions have so improved we do not need the amounts formerly required as assistance for the unemployed. They have told the different provinces that after the middle of July they will discontinue giving any more moneys for direct relief, that those moneys are not needed, and that the fifteenth of July will see the end of any necessity of the kind. On section 1-Power of commissioner of patents to grant patents.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to call attention to certain (particulars in reference to the bill itself and certain principles which I suggest should be followed by the committee in regard to a grave matter of public policy. The bill is entitled:
An act respecting patents on certain inventions of which Duplate Safety Glass Company of Canada, Limited, is entitled to the benefit.
I think I can show conclusively to the committee that the Duplate Safety Glass Company of Canada, Limited, is not entitled by law or by practice to the benefit of the several inventions which are covered by the patents the numbers of which as granted in Great Britain are set forth in the preamble. These several improvements with regard to the manufacture of glass were the inventions of certain inventors in France. In cooperation with the inventors in France two French companies at successive dates applied for and

Duplate Safety Glass Company
obtained fifteen patents covering certain processes in glass manufacture. Under a convention which was signed by Canada at The Hague on November 6, 1925, and ratified by Canada on May 1, 1928, it is provided in article 4 that any person who has deposited an application for a patent in any one of the contracting countries shall enjoy, for the purpose of deposit in other countries, and reserving the rights of third parties, a right of priority for the period of twelve months from the date of the deposit of the first application in any country which is a party to the convention. That is to say that within twelve months from the date on which an application was made in France for a patent the French inventor was entitled to apply in other countries which were parties to The Hague Convention for the Protection of Industrial Property for a patent in that country covering the same invention.
The French companies proceeded to apply for patents in the United States and patents in Great Britain. Although the United States is not a party to the union or to the convention, congress has provided by law that a foreign patentee, that is the inventor who obtains a foreign patent, may apply at the patent office at Washington for a patent covering the same invention. But in the United States the application must be made, as under the convention, within a term of twelve months; no further extension of time is allowed, and if the application is not made at Washington within twelve months then the invention falls into the public domain and is open to public use throughout that country. In Great Britain the same rule applies, because England is a party to this convention. If an application is made in France for a patent, then within twelve months from the date of the filing of the application in France the applicants must make application at the patent office in London if they desire to obtain a patent there.
It has been held by the exchequer court in a decision by Mr. Justice Audette in 1924 that in Canada an application may be made under the convention within twelve months from the date of the application in the foreign country -and I include Great Britain as a foreign country in that respect-but that under another subsection it is held that an application may be made here within two years from the date of the grant of the patent in the foreign country. That rule has been followed by the Canadian patent office. By that rule, allowing twelve months under the convention, and allowing two more years under the decision of
Mr. Justice Audette, applicants have practically three years from the date of the filing of the application in the foreign country within which to apply in Canada. Under that rule for a number of these patents the time within which application may be made in Canada has not yet expired. I shall refer to them by the English numbers, because although I have investigated and have the French numbers, the English numbers are placed in this bill, I think for purpose of camouflage and not otherwise. Patent No. 376219 still has under our law until October 11, 1934, within which application for a patent may be made at the patent office in Canada. Respecting patent No. 385843 the inventor has until January 5, 1935, to apply for a patent in Canada; respecting patent No. 393491 until December 31, 1934, within which to file an application for a patent in Canada; respecting patent No. 389314 until March 16, 1935, to apply for a patent in Canada. I therefore object to the house passing a special act providing for the granting of patents in Canada which are similar to foreign patents, when the applicants already have ample time within which to apply to the patent office in the ordinary way and have their applications investigated and decided upon by the commissioner. If the commissioner gives an erroneous decision then they can appeal from the commissioner to the Exchequer Court of Canada. I think as a matter of public policy we should not encourage applications to parliament for special acts providing for patents when the ordinary machinery of the patent act is still open to the applicants.
Those conditions, however, do not apply to the eleven other patents which are mentioned in the preamble to this bill. These eleven patents never have had force or effect in Canada. There is no right, title or interest outstanding in Canada with respect to those patents, to which any person in Canada or elsewhere can claim any beneficial interest whatsoever. They are patents which are, to use the ordinary phrase, in the public domain, and the inventions which they cover may be used by any manufacturer in Canada; they may be bought and sold in Canada without the payment of any royalty. The patent rights have never existed in Canada, and therefore no beneficial interest thereunder can be deemed to exist.
Patent No. 310838 was applied for in France on May 1, 1928. The applicants had twelve months within which to make applications in other countries under the convention, so the last day for an application for patent priority in Canada or in any other

country of the union was May 1, 1929. The applicants applied at Washington within the twelve month period and obtained a patent. They filed an application in Great Britain on March 18, 1929, and the patent was granted which is referred to by its English number in this preamble. Patent No. 340108 was applied for in France on March 13, 1929, and there were twelve months in which to obtain priority in Canada, which would be until March 13, 1930.
