This has been the result: allowing the applicants the twelve months from the date of the application in France; then allowing them what is not allowed by any other country of the union, but only allowed in Canada by reason of a decision given in 1924 by our exchequer court and a subsequent change in the act to conform to that decision, that is to say, one year from the date of the application, because usually a year elapses before the patent is granted, and also allowing them two more years from the granting of the patent in France or in England, wherever it was granted first, these eleven patents to which I have referred are out-dated in one case by five years and in other cases two years and nearly two years. So the time for each application in Canada has long since expired, and our act, under the interpretation which has been given to it, grants more widely extended privileges as to time than any other act to which I have been able to obtain access.
No application has been made to our patent office with regard to any of these patents. I have explained that applications may yet be made with regard to four of them, and my contention is that these patents should not be granted by a special act. Allowing the two extra years the time expired, for one of them at least five years ago; for another the time expired more than two years ago. In connection with others the time expired approximately two years or more ago. I have the dates, which have been worked out and with regard to which I need not trouble the house.
Though these patents never had existence in Canada, and though the time had elapsed within which applications could be made in Canada, on November 21, 1933, the Duplate

Safety Glass Company allege that they entered into a contract with Pilkington Brothers, of Liverpool, who are alleged to have previously acquired the English patents. The house is well aware that the English patent gave Pilkingtons no rights whatever in Canada; Canada happens to be an independent jurisdiction, in respect of patents. When the Duplate Safety Glass Company entered into a contract with Pilkingtons I am advised, and I think I can state it with absolute accuracy, that the Duplate Safety Glass Company were fully informed that there were no patent rights outstanding in Canada, and that, with regard to the eleven patents mentioned, the time had elapsed for the filing of applications here, including the first twelve months from the date of the application and the second term of two years from the date of the granting of the first patent. There was no deception whatever on the part of Pilkington Brothers. They disclosed all the facts to the Canadian company which is now promoting this bill. So that when the Canadian company applies to the House of Commons for this special legislation it is applying for a grant of a specific monopoly with regard to eleven inventions for the manufacture of glass, which inventions are now the property of the public. The main invention for five years, and the subsidiary inventions for terms of three and two years, may now be used at will by any manufacturer in Canada.
I suggest to hon. members that this is a case in which parliament should not intervene to create a private monopoly of the nature and extent of the one herewith proposed. As a matter of public policy I think this house should refuse to enact the measure. It is not an easy task for a minister of the crown to administer an office such as the patent office. It is fortunate that whenever the commissioner acting under the direction of the minister is in error, there is an appeal to the Exchequer Court of Canada in order that the remedy may be given by judicial decision. But that office is open to very grave temptations. I believe that the men now administering the office, although the temptations are great, are perfectly honest in their administration of it. But the applicants for this private monopoly, which it is now sought to create and establish in Canada by means of these patents, might just as well ask from the treasury of Canada a grant of 8150,000 or more, because if these patents, which are proposed to be established in Canada, were put up to public auction one might obtain very large cash considerations for them. However, they are not for .sale. They are the property of all those who are manufacturing

in Canada at the present time. But if this bill is enacted the Duplate Safety Glass Company of Canada, Limited, will have a monopoly of the manufacture under these fifteen patents. It will not only have a monopoly of the manufacturing, but if these glasswares are imported from the United States or France or England, where they are being manufactured, the importer will not only have to pay the customs duties imposed by parliament for revenue and for the protection of Canadian industry, but such importer can be compelled by the Duplate Company to pay a special royalty on every pound of glass of that nature imported into Canada. This glass is becoming of great importance in the automobile and elevator trades because it does not splinter as does ordinary glass, and under the suggested legislation the Duplate Glass Company may demand a royalty from every person in Canada who uses this glass either when imported from abroad, or made by any other manufacturer in Canada except the concern which is granted this special monopoly.
These being the facts I ask the House of Commons to consider whether or not, as a matter of public policy, this House of Commons should pass the bill. It is granting by legislative enactment a private monopoly covering fifteen inventions, a monopoly which would be subversive of the interests of all Canadian manufacturers of the same or similar products who are now entitled, of their own right, to import, to make or to use these products without payment of any licence fee or royalty to any person or company in any part of the world. I contend that the enactment of the proposed bill will enable the promoters, without any shadow of right or claim, except such as they may acquire under this special enactment, to demand and receive in Canada from importers, manufacturers and users, licence fees or royalties during the term of sixteen to eighteen years, to which they have no right, title or interest whatsoever. I contend that the creation of such a private monopoly by special legislation invariably tends prejudicially to affect and injure the industrial and commercial interests of Canada, and to impair the effective administration of the patent office which happens for the time being to be under my supervision, as Secretary of State, and which I am bound, by my oath of office, properly to administer. I do not wish to use too strong terms, but it seems to me that the passage of this measure would be a prostitution of the parliamentary powers conferred upon this parliament to promote the interests of a private monopoly which should not be created or allowed to exist.

Mr. Chairman, I should
like to speak on the bill before any final disposition is made. The bill in question, of which I am the sponsor in this house, seeks to extend the time under which applications for certain patents may be made. The Duplate Safety Glass Company of Canada, Limited, entered into a contract with the holders of certain French and British patents to have the right to manufacture the glass in this country and to have the exclusive right, as they then thought, under protective patents.
The glass is an invention of such a nature that upon being struck, instead of shattering and flying into pieces which may cut one or cause injury, it merely crumbles. In the private bills committee we had several demonstrations as to its usefulness.

This application was made because of an error on the part of two patent attorneys. The inventor instructed a French patent attorney to take out patents in France, the United Kingdoth and other countries, and the French patent attorney wrote a firm of patent attorneys in New York city and instructed them to take out patents in America. Unfortunately the attorneys in Washington or New York concluded that apparently America meant the United States, whereas the French attorney intended the whole of the North American continent, and notwithstanding the statement of the Secretary of State (Mr. Cahan) that he was informed at the time the deal was made the Duplate Glass Company had knowledge of the fact that these patents did not exist so far as Canadian patents are concerned, I can only say that the statement was made in the private bills committee that it was during the course of closing the deal for the acquisition of the Canadian patent rights that the Canadian company discovered that there were no Canadian patents, and hence this application.
The Secretary of State said that under the law where a patent application is refused by the patent commissioner an appeal may be had to the exchequer court, but certainly it will be obvious to all the legal members of this house that such an appeal can deal only with a question of law. If an inventor made application for a patent and the commissioner held, for example, that the invention was not patentable, then we might have
Duplate Safety Glass Company

aa appeal, but obviously when the time has expired within which you can make application there is no ground, upon which one can appeal to the exchequer court, and the purpose of this bill is to extend for a period of three months from its passing the time within which that application for a patent may be made to the commissioner .of patents.
Again there is considerable dispute on an interpretation of the act and the decision of the exchequer court to which the Secretary of State referred, as to just how long overdue this application is. I think I need not enter into any quarrel in that regard because, irrespective of that, the .principle of the bill is the same.
As to the four patents in respect of which it is alleged by the Secretary of State that they are still within time to apply, I have investigated the matter and I find that to be correct and when I conclude I shall move an amendment to strike out those patent numbers from the preamble to the bill, which will then allow the applicants to make their application in the ordinary way to the .patent office.
Prior to the discovery by the Duplate Glass Company that they were not protected with Canadian .patents they had made an investment in machinery and .plant for the purpose of manufacturing this glass in Canada of some $20,000. Needless to say, when they discovered the difficulty they ceased to continue a contemplated investment of $100,000 but have been manufacturing small quantities of this glass with the plant which they have available.
I should next like to point out to the house that there is nothing particularly new in a bill of this kind being brought before parliament. Before the private bills committee seven precedents were cited. It is within my recollection since I have been a member of this house that we have had such bills .before the committee, and on each occasion the question for decision by the committee and by parliament has been whether or not in the particular circumstances of each case an extension of time should .be granted.
The Secretary of State lays some emphasis on the question of monopoly. I will quite freely admit that if this bill is passed, and if in pursuance of this extension of time the commissioner of patents ultimately grants a patent, then it does create a monopoly, but it only creates the same kind of monopoly as is created in every single instance in which a patent is granted by this country in respect of any invention.

Will such a .monopoly be injurious? At the present time this glass is not manufactured in this country except to the limited extent of the investment of the Duplate Glass Company. It is imported from the United States and France, and even with the limited extent to which it is manufactured by the Duplate Glass Company at the present time the price at which it is offered for sale in this country is one-third less than the imported article. I am assured by the parties interested in procuring this bill that if they are allowed to have some protection in connection with this matter they will make an investment of somewhere between $100,000 and $150,000; that they will employ three or four times the number of .men who are now employed and that the glass will be on sale and available to the Canadian public at one-half the price they were paying for the imported article. Again I ask, will monopoly injure? I suppose the largest plate glass company in this country is the Consolidated Plate Glass Company. It was pointed out to me by the manager of that company that there is not a sufficient demand in Canada to support two manufacturers of safety glass. Consequently, although as alleged by the Secretary of State the right to make this glass has fallen into the public domain, nevertheless no one has sought to make it during these years that it has been in the public domain, and I fail to see how by giving protection to a firm that is now willing to make it, provide employment, and sell the article to the Canadian public at a price far less than the imported article, we are going to create a monopoly whch will be injurious to this country or how we are going to prostitute the powers of parliament.

Mr. Chairman, for fifteen years or more I have voiced opposition in the house to bills of this character. It is my conviction that during -many years past a number of such bills os this have been passed and patent rights established which, if all the facts had been fully understood by the members of the house and the public generally, would never have been granted.
I .think it should be borne in mind that the basic reason for the granting of a patent by the state is to preserve to some talented individual the right of his discovery. It is assumed that a discovery of some new and useful device or some scientific discovery or formula which will be of benefit to humanity may be made by an individual who is himself perhaps unable financially to promote the manufacture or production of the article, and that therefore there should be preserved to

Duplate Safety Glass Company
him some of the winnings, shall I say, that come from the discovery which he has made. And so, through all the years and I think in all countries, the idea of granting a patent is to preserve to the individual the benefits that go with the discovery that has been made. As time has passed and as industrial development has become more complex and on a much wider scale than was perhaps true of years ago, the value of patents has become less according to the ability of the individual to press forward the merits of his discovery or to bring it into general use. I think it has become increasingly difficult for individuals to get the full merit of patents. Very often large corporations will purchase for a comparatively small figure the rights of a patent, put it away and never use it because the new device is such that it might conflict with some article already on the market and well established in their industry. In dealing with matters of patents I think the major duty of parliament is to preserve the interests of the individual primarily responsible.
The article here dealt with is a certain type of glass, a new type of glass. This is something which is very generally used and which is needed or required by a large number of industries. It is alleged that a patent attorney in France made an error or committed an oversight when dealing with a patent attorney in New York and instructing him to take out patents in America. Because the patent attorney in New York did not safeguard the interests of his clients in Canada, it is argued that this group of individuals have a right to come to parliament and ask for the special legislation now before us. It is very difficult for me to believe that a patent attorney in France would be so, ignorant of what is necessary to establish hie rights in various parts of the world that he would overlook a place like Canada. I am quite certain that a patent attorney in Canada would not advise an attorney in Paris to look after his interests in other European countries, and then pay no more attention to the matter. I am quite certain that when the patent attorney in Paris got his returns from the patent attorney in New York he at once recognized that he had received protection in but one country, namely, the United States. In addition to the United States, there is Mexico on the one side and Canada on the other. It is difficult to conceive that such an error could be made, and it certainly does not appeal to me as the reason why parliament should pass a special act to vest this patent in the applicants.
The suggestion is made that the granting of this patent will possibly result in the establishment of a new industry in Canada. I certainly would like to see a new industry established in Canada but I cannot conceive why the failure to obtain these patent rights would deter a bona fide industry from entering upon the manufacture of this class of glass. I am not at the moment familiar with the rate of duty upon this article, but that rate would be the same whether or not there was a patent granted. So far as the particular industry is concerned, the protection would be precisely what the tariff provides. In my opinion there is no argument in that contention. The only additional advantage to the applicants would be to obtain the exclusive right of manufacture in Canada, and that exclusive right of manufacture would mean the charging of royalties to those who desired either to make or use this glass. The advantage to anyone who wished to manufacture this glass in Canada of securing this special bill authorizing the issue of this patent would be that he could charge higher prices for the glass because he had a patent. I cannot follow my hon. friend in his argument in that respect. My hon. friend said that it would likely result in the cutting of the price of glass, but here again I find it difficult to follow him because the only difference in the price of glass would be the amount of the royalty, and that could be cut only if the individual securing the patent rights were to make the price of glass so much higher than otherwise would be necessary.
For a great many years I have raised my voice in this house in opposition to this class of bill. I feel it is unwise and very often improvident for this house to give these special rights. Very often we are asked to revive a patent which has completely expired. If I remember rightly, a patent right expires in Canada after eighteen years, which is two years longer than in Great Britain. We are frequently asked to extend this right because an article has not been manufactured or for some other reason. I think parliament should be exceedingly careful in these matters. I reiterate what I said a moment ago. In the first place, the object of a patent right is to protect the interests of the individual who makes the discovery. The assumption is that if the individual does not take advantage of his patent right within a reasonable time-I have forgotten the exact time, but I think it is two or three years-the right then expires and it becomes, as the Secretary of State (Mr Cahan) has so well defined, part of the public domain. I am sorry that I must differ with the hon. member who is sponsoring this bill but I take very strong exception to its passage. I do this, first, because of the general principles
Duplate Safety Glass Company

which I have indicated, and, second, because of the specific reasons which are inherent to this particular case, and which have been so ably put forward by the Secretary of State. I regret to say that as far as I am concerned I shall have to express my opposition to the bill by voting against it.

Mr. Chairman, for once at least I find myself in hearty agreement with the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens). He has outlined the reasons why patents are granted. I am heartily in sympathy with the principle of the granting of patents to men who have invented something useful for humanity. I think they should be allowed to reap in a large measure the benefit of their skill and industry. I am not nearly so favourably inclined to the large companies which secure patents from individuals. I think it is a well known fact that many clever inventors have lost almost the entire fruits of their inventions because they have been grabbed up by some of the big moneyed powers. When we come to deal with large companies or corporations I am not so leniently inclined as I would be towards a private individual. It is true that parliament on a number of occasions has passed special bills reviving patents which have been allowed to lapse because of some slight error. I have been in the private bills committee now for a number of years and on several occasions we have had such questions to deal with. But it seems to me that the circumstances surrounding this particular patent are very different from anything we have had before us up to the present time. I can scarcely imagine, as the Minister of Trade and Commerce has pointed out, that the attorney in Paris would be so completely ignorant as has been suggested he might be. I know that in regard to many of the cases that have come before us I have had some hesitation in voting for an extension of the time during which a patent might be acquired; for in some instances it did seem that the attorney who had the matter in hand had not taken action, or had failed to take action until it seemed desirable in the interests of those for whom; he was asking that action should be taken. However, I shall not go into that matter at any length.
Undoubtedly this particular patent is a matter of great interest to the Canadian people. The granting of a monopoly to this company for a period of sixteen or eighteen years would unquestionably place a heavy impost upon the Canadian people. The hon. member who is promoting the bill has made an argument which it seems to me will scarcely 
stand investigation. He tells us that the company is now manufacturing in small quantities and selling that glass at half the price of the imported article. Well, if it is doing that and can do that, why can it not continue to do it? The company has the protection of the duty, but it wants not only the protection which undoubtedly our friends on the other side would be willing to accord it, though we will not enter into that question at the moment, but also the right to collect a royalty on all glass imported. I ask any hon. gentleman in this house,, does he for a moment seriously believe that a company which is now manufacturing this glass at half the price of the imported article will continue to manufacture it and sell it at that price when it has the exclusive monopoly, when it has not only the protection accorded by the tariff but also the right to collect royalties? For my part I certainly intend to oppose the bill.
For the same reasons which in the private bills committee warranted my voting against the bill, I will vote against it now.

Mr. Speaker, I think that this bill No. 113 is introduced for a political purpose. On September 11, 1930, at the special session, I requested work to relieve unemployment in the town of St. John's which I have the honour of representing in the house. To a question I put to the hon. Minister of Marine (Mr. Duranleau), whom I am pleased to see in his seat this evening, he replied:
As to the second' question asked by the hon. member: the deepening of the Richelieu river, my views on the subject are well known. I believe that this river should become a means of transportation from the St. Lawrence to lake Champlain, and I trust that I shall have the support of my colleagues in connection with this matter, as soon as it is found possible to act.
The hon. Minister of Marine certainly could have found it possible, under those circumstances, to fulfil his promises of the special session of 1930. In the course of the last electoral campaign, the hon. minister, who represents Chambly-Vercheres in the House, made promises of which some hon. members reminded him, he replied, at the time, that he could not remember having made such a statement. I trust he will not deny the excerpt which I have just quoted and whicn can be found at page 132 of Hansard, September 11, 1930. The hon. minister would have been worthy of praise had he remembered the Chambly canal.
I note in the Annex A of this bill an amount of $40,000 for St. Lambert. In 1931, an amount of $69,000, included in the appropriations for unemployment work, was expended in St. Lambert on a retaining wall. Of the $20,000,000 voted at the special session of 1930, $415,000 only was expended in the province of Quebec yet the county of Chambly-Vercheres obtained $129,000 of that amount. The hon. minister could have, under the circumstances, remembered the Chambly canal. I think that $40,000 would have been better expended in improving that canal than by building a retaining wall at St. Lambert; it would also prove more profitable to the hon. minister, at the next election. The Chambly canal has been neglected for a few years past. Last year, hardly 100 boats passed through it during the summer. This year, for the first time, ever since I remember, the water was let in the canal on June 1. If the hon. minister, according to his statement, had wished to carry out the Liberal party's program, the oppor-

It would have been a worthy act to carry on this work and not to allow the outlay already made in the Richelieu river to be a total loss.
I note in the Annex an amount of $35,500 for Lacolle and another amount of $31,500 for Cantic. Ever since the advent of the Conservative party to power in 1930, we have tried without success to have this work done, unfortunately, these localities are represented by a Liberal member and we have no chance whatever of succeeding. Since the redistribution of counties last year, the parish of Lacolle has been included in the county of Chateau-guay-Huntingdon, and I note that $67,000 has been appropriated solely for Lacolle and $3,500 for Huntingdon-$70,500 for a county as large as my hand.
This afternoon, the leader of the Liberal party stated that this bill was introduced with a political end in view. The hon. member for Laurier-Outremont (Mr. Mercier) analysed the work proposed for the province of Quebec, going over the entire schedule, and our hon. friends opposite cannot deny that this work is being done with a political end in view.
I note that there is an item of $272,000 for Three Rivers. By this act, the hon. Minister of Marine perhaps intends to carry out the promises he made in 1931 and which were not fufilled up to date; however, this amount of $272,000 for Three Rivers is not sufficiently large to save the hon. member who represents that county to-day. Moreover, the outlay of $40,000 in St. Lambert will be of no avail to the hon. Minister of Marine to save him at the next election.
Work was requested by the town of Iberville which suffers from unemployment, for instance, work to improve the wharf of that locality. If there is one place in this country where money should be expended to improve a wharf, it is certainly at Iberville. That town is quite important. All are aware that the Richelieu is a beautiful and navigable river. Iberville possesses an old wharf only 75 to 100 foot in length. Requests were made on various occasions, in 1931, 1932, 1933 and 1934. Unfailingly the answer was: There is no money. Under the present circumstances, it would have been an act worthy of praise. If this program of public works had not had a political end in view, certainly the town of Iberville would have been remembered and the Chambly canal would have been improved. The hon. minister is aware that this

canal is very important. It was for Chambly-Bassin and Chambly-Canton a source of revenue which does not exist to-day because they are neglected and no improvement is made.
Some attempt was made, hardly a few
months ago, to obtain funds from the Department of Railways and Canals to make improvement along the Chambly Canal which borders the national highway from Rouse's Point to Montreal. By improving the Chambly Canal, by dredging and building wharves, it would have been possible to widen the road. Very little material would have been required and it would have provided much work to the unemployed of the town of St John's. Within the last four years the town of St. John's has expended each year between $40,000 and $50,000 to relieve its unemployed. The government should not have granted favours but shown a sense of fairness towards the county of St. John's. Such was not the case, I am aware that this measure has a political end in view, nothing else.
Last winter, work was carried out on the locks at St. John's and along the canal. However, no work was given to the unemployed. To be employed on the Chambly canal it was absolutely necessary to have a letter of recommendation from the Conservative candidate so that men from Chambly and elsewhere were brought over there thus depriving the unemployed at St John's. Probably, because there are too many Liberals in St. John's; I can see no other reason. I state that it is a shabby procedure, on the part of the Conservative party, to refuse work to unemployed, heads of families, simply because they are supposed to be Liberals, while work was given to sons of Conservatives whose fathers were working and in no way were in want. When there were more than 350 unemployed receiving the dole, work was refused to these people because it was absolutely necessary that their applications be approved by the defeated candidate. As the latter is acquainted with every one and knows to what party they belong, those who were supposed to be Liberals were out of luck. The proof that these public works have a political end in view is that the government delayed introducing this bill until after the elections of Ontario and Saskatchewan, under the plea that they did not wish to influence the people of those provinces. In the county of Brome-Missisquoi, at Farniham, a beautiful little town, $58,000 will be expended for a public building. No reason is given. At Huntingdon, the wealthiest county of Quebec, where public

works are the least required, S70,000 is granted. I therefore protest, sir, and contend that such public works have a political object in view.

Almost every member on both sides of the house, I believe, is agreed that the effort to provide employment through a public works program is very desirable. But in this program it is evident to me at least that the needs of the provinces have not been considered very carefully, at any rate the province from which I come has not received anything like equal treatment with the other provinces. I note that out of some S40,000,000 the amount allotted to British Columbia is just over $2,000,000. Might I draw attention to the fact that over $2,000,000 is allotted to one city alone in Canada, and more than to the whole of the province of British Columbia. The Prime Minister at various times has chided us for raising the cry of east against west, but when I look over this program of works I cannot help but feel that in the west, and particularly British Columbia, there is some justification for that cry. I would point out that so far this year $9,000,000 has been provided for the development of harbours and rivers on the Atlantic side of this country and only some $273,200 for the ports on the Pacific coast. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, is it any wonder that we rise in our places and ask when are we in British Columbia going to receive anything like the same treatment that has been accorded this year and almost every year since confederation in expenditures looking to the building up of the Atlantic coast? I repeat that this same state of things has already happened this year-almost nine millions appropriated for the Atlantic side and only a little over a quarter of a million for the Pacific coast.
Dealing with the bill before us I am not going to repeat what has been said by various speakers, that certain districts and certain provinces have been favoured over others. I am not going to say a great deal about what has been given to the city of Calgary, but it is interesting to note that over one million dollars, or more than fifty per cent of what the whole of British Columbia is to receive, is to be expended in the city of Calgary. Further I am not unmindful of the fact that considerable sums were spent for buildings in that city in 1930. If it were a question of providing works where necessary I would draw this to the attention of the minister- and I might say the various parts of the program I have in my hand have been given to both the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Stewart) and the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett). Speaking of one, we have in the city of New Westminster a post office which was constructed in the year 1900 when there were only some 10,000 people in that city. Since then the district has grown until to-day some
60.000	people are served by that post office. So acute are conditions for those who have to deal with postal matters there that an annex has been provided close to the main building, and I am going to tell the minister of the conditions existing in that annex. The size of the annex is twenty-one by forty-two feet, and in it there are housed forty-three people. Bear in mind that this is an outside building. The parcel post and letter carrier deliveries have been inaugurated since the main building was erected. The rapid growth in population not only of the city of New Westminster, but of the surrounding district has made conditions for the workers there terrible, and it is no exaggeration to use the word. I have visited there; I was there before coming to Ottawa. I am surprised that they have had to carry on for so long in such cramped quarters. There are also three rural mail routes totalling some ninety miles, on which the volume of mail is very heavy. The main post office building is a one story structure. The ground for the extension was purchased many years ago; plans were drawn up and submitted to the department; they were O.K.'d by the postal authorities, but nothing has been done about it.
The minister may say, "Why was it not done when the Liberal administration was in power?" I can only say that if it had been my privilege to be here they would have heard about it. I am holding no brief for what was done or not done previous to 1930; I can only speak for the time I have been in the house, but certainly this situation should not have been overlooked. The minister may say that in the present bill some

I was interested in following the discussion as to fair wages, and I noted that the minister rose to say that this was provided for. I would remind the minister that while that provision may be in the Public Works Act my experience would indicate that the contractors find ways of getting around that law. I drew one case to the attention of the minister, where a contract was let for rock work in the Fraser river. The work was sublet to another contractor, who paid only half the wages the first contractor would have had to pay under the fair wage clause. When I got after the dominion government about it the minister admitted that he did not know' a great deal about that contract which had been sublet. It may be provided in the act that no contract shall be sublet without the authority of the minister, but I know that has been done in the past. Contracts involving considerable sums of money have been let to subcontractors who have cut the wages in two, which permitted the contractor to make large profits. I had another case in connection with the shingling of the armoury in New Westminster. The regular price for shinglers was, I believe, eighty cents an hour.
